description: The dependency dashboard is on: it is the only place that shows what Renovate tried and could not land, which the weekly pull request never mentions.

vulnerabilityAlerts.description: Off, so that a vulnerability fix rides in the one weekly pull request like every other raise instead of arriving on its own branch outside the schedule.

lockFileMaintenance.description: Both lock files regenerated the day after the raises, which is where the transitive crates move.

packageRules.description: One pull request for everything, majors included. Every check has to pass before anything merges, so separate pull requests would only be that many rounds of CI for one week's raises.
steamcmd's version is a Unix timestamp, so every raise is a jump of thousands; best-practices refuses any major jump above 500 as a guard against date-like versions, which this is on purpose.
Cargo.toml names the version tested, not a floor, so a raise moves it along with the lock file.

steamcmd.description: Valve's manifest is KeyValues, not JSON, so it is read as plain text, one release per line, and the transform keeps the one line that holds the version.

customManagers.description: Rust: the toolchain CI and developers build with, and the rust-version the crate declares, which is the same version on purpose.

Valve's steamcmd manifests, one per system, pinned byte for byte in pins/. Only the version inside a pin can be raised here; the pins check in CI then fails on the stale packages and says to run `cargo run --example pins`, which rewrites the pin from Valve's live manifest for review.
A release tag with the SHA-256 of the asset downloaded on the next line: actionlint and cargo-deny. The tag and the digest move together.
A crate installed by version in a workflow: cargo-fuzz.
The runner images inside a job matrix, which the github-actions manager does not read.
